subtopic: Classification of Data and Frequency Distribution
stem: 6, 10, 10.5, 11, 15.5, 19, 20, 12, 13 are the given observations. By taking classes 6-10, 11-15, 16-20 prepare grouped frequency distribution table.
solution:
Using the inclusive classes 6-10, 11-15, 16-20 :

| Classes | Frequency (f) |
|---|---|
| 6-10 | 2 |
| 11-15 | 3 |
| 16-20 | 2 |

In the above table, we could not include the observations 10.5 and 15.5, because they fall between two classes and belong to none of 6-10, 11-15, 16-20. Only 7 of the 9 observations are counted.
Hence, in order to include them, we have to change the structure of the classes. If we take the class intervals as 5-10, 10-15, 15-20 the problem will be solved: 10.5 can go in 10-15 and 15.5 in 15-20. But a question still arises - in which interval should the score 10 be included, 5-10 or 10-15 ? To overcome the difficulty we follow a convention: the UPPER class limit of a class is excluded from that class, so 10 is placed in 10-15. This is called the exclusive method of classification.
Taking the classes accordingly :

| Class interval (Marks) | Frequency (No. of students) |
|---|---|
| 5-10 | 1 |
| 10-15 | 5 |
| 15-20 | 2 |
| 20-25 | 1 |

Now all 9 observations are counted.

stem:
The first unit test of 40 marks was conducted for a class of 35 students. The marks obtained by the students were as follows. Find the mean of the marks.
40, 35, 30, 25, 23, 20, 14, 15, 16, 20, 17, 37,
37, 20, 36, 16, 30, 25, 25, 36, 37, 39, 39, 40,
15, 16, 17, 30, 16, 39, 40, 35, 37, 23, 16.
solution:
Here we can add all the observations, but it will be a tedious job. Three students obtained 30 marks each, so their sum is \(30 + 30 + 30 = 90\), which is \(30 \times 3\). In this way the sum of the marks of all the students is worked out in the following table, where \(x_i\) is a score and \(f_i\) is the number of students who got it.

| Marks \(x_i\) | No. of students \(f_i\) | \(f_i \times x_i\) |
|---|---|---|
| 14 | 1 | 14 |
| 15 | 2 | 30 |
| 16 | 5 | 80 |
| 17 | 2 | 34 |
| 20 | 3 | 60 |
| 23 | 2 | 46 |
| 25 | 3 | 75 |
| 30 | 3 | 90 |
| 35 | 2 | 70 |
| 36 | 2 | 72 |
| 37 | 4 | 148 |
| 39 | 3 | 117 |
| 40 | 3 | 120 |
| Total | \(N = 35\) | \(\sum f_i x_i = 956\) |

\(\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum f_i x_i}{N} = \dfrac{956}{35} = 27.31\) marks (approximately)
So the mean of the given data is 27.31.

stem: Find the median of 54, 63, 66, 72, 98, 87, 92.
solution:
Let us write the given observations in ascending order :
54, 63, 66, 72, 87, 92, 98
There are 7 observations, an odd number, so one score stands exactly in the middle.
Here the 4th number is at the middle position, which is 72.
\(\therefore\) Median of the scores \(= 72\)

stem: Find the median of the data 30, 25, 32, 23, 42, 36, 40, 33, 21, 43.
solution:
Let us write the given observations in ascending order :
21, 23, 25, 30, 32, 33, 36, 40, 42, 43
Here the number of observations is 10, which is an even number.
\(\therefore\) the 5th and 6th numbers are in the middle position. Those numbers are 32 and 33.
\(\therefore\) Median \(= \dfrac{32 + 33}{2} = \dfrac{65}{2} = 32.5\)

If the data is arranged in ascending order, it is easy to find the observation repeating the maximum number of times.
Ascending order of the given data : 35, 40, 55, 55, 55, 67, 75, 75, 90, 95
The observation repeated the maximum number of times is 55 (three times; 75 occurs only twice).
\(\therefore\) The mode for the given data is 55.

stem:
The ages of workers in a certain factory are given in the following table. Find the mode of their ages.

| Age (Year) | 19 | 21 | 25 | 27 | 30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Workers | 5 | 15 | 13 | 15 | 7 |
solution:
Here the maximum frequency is 15; but this frequency belongs to TWO observations, 21 and 27.
\(\therefore\) Mode \(= 21\) and \(27\), so the mode for the ages is 21 years and 27 years.
(A set of data may have more than one mode. Such data is called bimodal.)

stem: What is the class-mark of class 25-35 ?
_why: Class mark \(= \dfrac{\text{lower class limit} + \text{upper class limit}}{2} = \dfrac{25 + 35}{2} = \dfrac{60}{2} = 30\). Option C is the numerator left undivided.

stem: If the classes are 0-10, 10-20, 20-30... then in which class should the observation 10 be included ?
_why: These are continuous classes, so the exclusive method applies: the upper class limit of a class is EXCLUDED from that class. Hence 10 does not belong to 0-10 but to 10-20. Option C would count the same observation twice, which is exactly what the convention exists to prevent.

context: Write the correct alternative answer for each of the following questions.
stem: If \(\bar{x}\) is the mean of \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\) and \(\bar{y}\) is the mean of \(y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n\) and \(\bar{z}\) is the mean of \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n\) then \(\bar{z} = ?\)
_why: The sum of the x's is \(n\bar{x}\) and the sum of the y's is \(n\bar{y}\), and together there are \(2n\) observations. So \(\bar{z} = \dfrac{n\bar{x} + n\bar{y}}{2n} = \dfrac{\bar{x} + \bar{y}}{2}\). The n cancels, which is why the two options carrying an n are wrong.

context: Write the correct alternative answer for each of the following questions.
stem: The mean of five numbers is 80, out of which mean of 4 numbers is 46, find the 5th number :
_why: 5th number = (sum of all five) - (sum of the four) = 5 x 50 - 4 x 46 = 250 - 184 = 66, reading the first mean as 50 (see the misprint note). With the printed 80 the answer would be 5 x 80 - 4 x 46 = 216, which is not among the options.

context: Write the correct alternative answer for each of the following questions.
stem: Mean of 100 observations is 40. The 9th observation is 30. If this is replaced by 70 keeping all other observations same, find the new mean.
_why: The old sum is \(100 \times 40 = 4000\). Replacing 30 by 70 raises the sum by 40, to 4040, so the new mean is \(4040 \div 100 = 40.4\). Only the CHANGE of 40 matters, spread over 100 observations, which is 0.4.
